decisions.decision: Compatibility is defined as TWO relations, both named, neither collapsed into the other. R1 is between a Provider CLI version and an ADAPTER: SupportedCLIVersions(adapter) is a declared, closed, half-open interval per adapter in internal/provider, pinned to the argv surface and envelope shape that adapter actually implements. R2 is between the adapter contract and the LOOP version: SupportedLoopVersions(contract) is a declared interval over the Loop's own release identity, keyed to provider.ContractVersion. The capability's 対応version is R1's interval and its 対応Loop Version is R2's interval; a verdict is the conjunction, and it is unknown whenever either input is absent. Compatibility is deliberately NOT defined directly between a Provider CLI version and a Loop version.
decisions.rationale: The relation must be between the version and the thing that breaks, and the thing that breaks is measured: the argv each adapter emits (internal/provider/adapters.go:75-83) and the envelope parseFixture accepts with DisallowUnknownFields (adapters.go:141-149). The three cli-version-incompatible fixtures are exactly a declared-version envelope carrying a field the adapter's shape does not declare, and internal/provider/adapters_test.go:258 already asserts all three produce FailureContract. A Loop version does not parse an envelope; an adapter does. Defining the relation Provider-CLI-to-Loop directly would force a new compatibility row for every Loop release that changed nothing about any adapter, and would make two Loop versions carrying byte-identical adapters report different compatibility -- which is false and would eventually be corrected by widening some interval, i.e. by weakening the statement. Keying R2 to provider.ContractVersion rather than to a per-adapter value is also measured rather than chosen: ContractVersion = "v1" (internal/provider/provider.go:18) is already the value WorkPacket.Validate (provider.go:60) and Handoff.Validate (handoff.go:182) refuse a mismatch on, so it is already the contract identity that crosses a handoff.

decisions.decision: Authority is assigned per fact, and no self-claim is authority anywhere. (a) Which Provider CLI versions an adapter supports: the source-declared interval in internal/provider, and nothing a CLI reports about itself. (b) Which Loop versions carry that adapter contract: the Loop's own release identity read through internal/application's existing ReleaseObserver, and not a Runner's self-report. (c) What version a CLI actually is on a machine: the owner-approved, digest-bound provider-preflight record's provider.version, measured by that record's own --version verification argv, and not a version string inside a Provider response envelope. (d) Whether the declared support statement is TRUE of a real CLI: nothing in this repository; only a live exercise, and V2-028 owns it.
decisions.rationale: This is V2-069 d5's rule applied to a second kind of claim, and applying it consistently is what stops the surface from drifting into self-certification. V2-069's own words are that a report is 'a self-claim about bytes the Control Plane never receives' and that no admission path may read it; a Provider CLI's declared version is the same class of claim, one machine further away. Row (b) is measured rather than assumed available: internal/application already reads the release identity through AttachReleaseObserver / ReleaseState, and ErrReleaseObserverNotConfigured (internal/application/release_surface.go:41) states in its own message that a process without an explicit release source root 'can report no release version' -- so the Loop version is itself sometimes absent, which is why d3's verdict enum must carry unknown rather than defaulting. Row (c) picks the preflight record over the response envelope because the record's value is bound by an approval digest and re-verified by CostLedger.Reserve before a process starts, while an envelope value is whatever the Provider chose to print. Row (d) is forced by gate rules G3.1 and G3.3, which V2-027's evidence already quotes: unit, fake, stub and contract-fixture evidence satisfies no real-environment condition at any grade.

decisions.decision: Both intervals and both verdicts are reported on the existing Provider registry entry, and no field spells compatible without unknown being a sibling value. A new compatibility block carries the declared R1 interval, the declared R2 interval, the observed Loop version or its absence, a loop_compatibility verdict in {compatible, incompatible, unknown} and a cli_compatibility verdict in the same closed set whose value is unknown unless the Loop's own execution path has observed a contract-incompatible failure for that Provider. No numeric threshold and no monetary term appears in it.
decisions.rationale: V2-069 d7's rule, stated there as 'no field or enum value spells compatible without unknown being a sibling value', is the only shape in which a compatibility report is honest here, and this surface needs it twice rather than once because the two relations have independently-absent inputs: the Loop version is absent when no release observer is configured, and the observed CLI version never reaches the control plane at all (d4). The vocabulary ban is inherited rather than re-argued: V2-067 d6 forbids budget, quota, billing, spend, cost and credit in any read-model field name or enum value and asserts it mechanically over the emitted JSON keys, and dp-v2-027's usage window forbids the same set plus price and usd in identifiers, so the new block must be scanned by both existing scans rather than by a new one.

decisions.decision: No observed Provider CLI version is transported to the control plane, and no request DTO is widened. The observed-CLI side of the verdict reaches the registry only through the failure class the Loop's own execution path already reports: provider_observation.failure_class = contract-incompatible on POST /v1/executions/result, which already exists and already maps to health unavailable and blocked_reason last-invocation-failed-non-retryably.
decisions.rationale: Widening the observation is not available: internal/application/provider_registry_test.go:1442 asserts ProviderObservationInput's fields are exactly [Name FailureClass StoppedForInspection], so a fourth field turns an existing test red, which this task may not do. A sibling object on the same request would satisfy the letter of that test while defeating its purpose, and would have no producer either, since no Runner in this repository posts anything (V2-069 d10 measured that cmd/runner/main.go refuses to run without --fake and internal/runner contains no net/http). And it is not needed: the capability clause asks the owner to see 対応version and 対応Loop Version, which are the declared intervals the repository genuinely owns, plus a compatibility state -- and the incompatible state is already observable through a class the pipeline already carries end to end. Choosing the existing path over a new one means the incompatible case is reportable today rather than after a Runner client exists, which is the difference between a surface that works and a surface that is ready to work.

decisions.decision: The handoff trigger is neither a FailureClass nor a window state alone: it is the negation of a declared Sendable predicate over three inputs -- the breaker's circuit state, the usage window's state, and the pool slot's state -- evaluated for the source Provider. Sendable(P) holds when the circuit reports sending, the window is not exhausted, and the slot is available or in use. The trigger is Sendable(source) being false.
decisions.rationale: Each of the three alternatives was checked against the tables already in the tree and each fails on a specific row. FailureClass alone contradicts three rows of the d12 opening table (internal/provider/breaker.go:104-126): cancelled and invalid-input are declared there as 'not an observation about the Provider' and must never move work; transport, timeout and unknown are count-toward-windowed-threshold, so handing off on the first occurrence would defeat the threshold that exists precisely to avoid reacting to one blip; and model opens only the narrower Provider-and-model circuit, whose stated prescribed action is to evaluate other model candidates in the same pool, which is impossible if the whole Provider moved. The breaker's state alone is necessary but not sufficient, because exhausting our own attempt ceiling is not a Provider fault and produces no FailureClass, so the window's exhausted state reaches nothing today -- a measured gap. The window's state alone is insufficient and dangerous, because WindowUnknown means an invocation reported no usage at all (internal/provider/usagewindow.go:216-227) and rounding unknown to exhausted would move work on an absence of information. Making the breaker the primary input also keeps one authority: RequestFromHandoff already gates the TARGET on CircuitSending (handoff.go:238-240), so using a different authority for the source would make one handoff consult two.

decisions.decision: The window's exhausted state is folded in as a distinct non-failure reason, and NOT by opening the breaker. No FailureClass is synthesized for it, the d12 table is not edited, and ApplyObservation's behaviour is unchanged; Sendable simply reads the window directly alongside the circuit.
decisions.rationale: Opening the circuit requires a FailureClass -- open() records obs.Failure.Class in c.because (breaker.go:395) and every report carries those classes as its stated reason -- so routing an own-ceiling exhaustion through the breaker would require inventing a class for it. Every candidate class is a lie: quota would claim the Provider signalled exhaustion when it did not, unknown would claim we could not classify something we classified exactly, and a new class would need a row in the opening table and would then appear in Because as though the Provider had done something. The window's own doc comment already draws this line for a different reason -- it 'never decides whether a process may start', that authority being the cost ledger's alone -- so reading it as one input to a selection decision is the use it was built for, while making it open a circuit is not.

decisions.decision: A measured defect is closed as part of this task: a Provider whose pool slot is unauthenticated has a CLOSED circuit and therefore passes RequestFromHandoff today, so the existing code path can hand work to a Provider with no authenticated session. The fix is that Sendable reads the slot state and that the new decision function is the only producer of a handoff target; RequestFromHandoff's signature and behaviour are left exactly as they are, and an AST guard asserts it is referenced from exactly one non-test location.
decisions.rationale: The defect is arithmetic from three measured facts: NewBreaker creates every circuit in phaseClosed regardless of the slot (breaker.go:218-223), Report maps phaseClosed to CircuitSending (breaker.go:245-248), and ApplyObservation's ActionMoveSlotWithoutOpening branch touches only the pool (breaker.go:367-370). So after an observed provider-unauthenticated failure the slot is SlotUnauthenticated while the circuit still reports sending, and RequestFromHandoff -- which consults only the breaker -- accepts it. That directly violates non_goal 2. Widening RequestFromHandoff's parameters would be the obvious fix and is rejected for a measurable reason: it breaks compilation of the existing call sites in internal/provider/handoff_test.go, so those tests could not keep passing under their own names with their own assertions unchanged. The single-producer plus AST-guard shape is the idiom this repository already uses for exactly this problem -- internal/runner/source_guard_test.go:227 pins ProcessSupervisor to one referenced location so that a second execution path cannot appear unnoticed -- and it makes the gate structural rather than advisory. The residual (a caller who hand-picks a target and calls RequestFromHandoff directly) is recorded with its owner rather than hidden.

decisions.decision: The wiring is structural, and this is the difference between this task and V2-069's reported-but-ungated intersection. DecideHandoff is the single function that may produce a handoff target: it evaluates Sendable for the source, filters candidates by authorization, Sendable, declared compatibility and the attempt history, and returns a closed disposition in {none, handoff-proposed, waiting} with a target or a closed waiting reason. No handoff Request can be constructed without passing it, because it is the only producer of a target and RequestFromHandoff is asserted to have exactly one non-test caller.
decisions.rationale: The task's outcome says decide AND wire, and the measured starting point is that nothing is wired at all: a search for NewPool, NewBreaker, NewUsageWindow, ApplyObservation, PrepareHandoff, ChainHandoff and RequestFromHandoff across every *.go file outside internal/provider returns hits in that package's own tests and nowhere else -- not even internal/runner constructs a pool. So the honest question is not 'which existing caller do we change' but 'what makes the decision unavoidable in the absence of a caller', and the answer is single-producer plus enforced single-consumer. That genuinely gates, unlike V2-069's intersection, which is computed and compared against nothing because no canonical schema counter exists. It also does not overclaim: a Runner's selection loop still does not exist, and the evidence must say so plainly rather than implying that production hands off today.

decisions.decision: The pre-invocation compatibility refusal is expressed where a Request is built, not where a process starts: provider.Request gains one optional field, CLIVersionDeclared, and the shared build helper refuses fail-closed when that field is non-empty and measured outside the adapter's declared interval. An empty field is unknown and never refuses. internal/runner is not edited at all.
decisions.rationale: The refusal must be reachable before an invocation is spent, because discovering an incompatibility through Parse costs one real invocation against a Provider the Loop already knows it cannot parse. build (internal/provider/adapters.go:22-48) is the one place all three adapters funnel through and already performs exactly this kind of pre-argv refusal for a traversal segment, so the check lands beside the checks it belongs with rather than in a new gate. Refusing on measured-incompatible while never refusing on unknown is two different fail directions in one function and both are deliberate: fail closed on invoking a known-incompatible CLI, fail open on reporting, because rounding unknown to incompatible would take a Provider out of service on an absence of information. Not editing internal/runner is a scope decision with a measured cost: internal/runner is inside the file set the representative Provider's live exercise compiles (.agents/v2/evidence/artifacts/V2-075-live-exercise-files.json), so touching it would force a live re-observation onto this task on top of everything else. The consequence -- that with no caller supplying CLIVersionDeclared the pre-invocation refusal is exercised by tests and not by production -- is recorded and attributed rather than papered over.

decisions.decision: The decision table is declared twice, in internal/provider and in internal/application, over one shared normalised input tuple, and a by-value pinning test compares the two cell by cell. internal/application does not import internal/provider.
decisions.rationale: ci/components.json declares application's dependencies as [domain, infra, release], so an import of internal/provider would be an undeclared edge that internal/ci's manifest derivation turns into a red make check, and only V2-045 may declare one. The repository has already solved this problem three times in the same way and this task follows it rather than inventing a fourth: V2-067 d2 pins the three Provider names independently in internal/provider and internal/application, V2-069 d12 re-declares internal/update's semver and 64-hex patterns as literals in internal/application with TestRunnerVersionShapesArePinnedToTheUpdatePatterns as the only thing that catches drift, and internal/provider's own breaker keeps its Loop-taxonomy mapping as a declared table in breaker_test.go rather than as an import. The two sides necessarily start from different observations -- internal/provider sees a circuit, a window and a slot, internal/application sees health, blocked_reason, runaway state and concurrency -- so the pinning must be over a shared normalised tuple rather than over the raw inputs, and each side's mapping onto that tuple must be total over its own closed enums. The drift risk is real and is named in the risks rather than dismissed.

decisions.decision: No new port and no store change. The registry's disposition is derived entirely from state the registry already reads in one bounded keyed read per Provider: the observation ring, its VerifiedAt, the assignment ring (which already carries IncrementID, so 'already tried for this Increment' is derivable), the standing authorization, the runaway state and the concurrency allocation. If the implementer finds a stored fact is missing, that is a stop-and-escalate, not a new port.
decisions.rationale: This is the decision that keeps the task tractable and it is measured, not hoped: ProviderAssignment already declares IncrementID (internal/application/provider_registry.go:425-430) and AppendProviderAssignment keeps a bounded ring per Provider, so the set of Providers already tried for one Increment is a fold over data the read already returns. Adding a port would oblige both store adapters to implement it, which is dp-v2-067's recorded risk 2 -- the Firestore adapter's read cost is gated by docs/architecture/validation.md section 5 and a naive per-read scan would break the constant-cost property the existing measurement (one GET /v1/providers reads a constant number of documents regardless of Requirement count) was built to prove. Deriving instead of storing also keeps this task out of both store adapters, which removes two of the six surface-chain file groups from its footprint.

decisions.decision: The waiting reason vocabulary is derived mechanically as exactly one reason per cell of the decision table whose disposition is waiting, and it is a DIFFERENT vocabulary from the queue waiting reason V2-068 introduces. A test asserts the two vocabularies share no member and that neither is empty.
decisions.rationale: V2-068's outcome is 'a queue summary that reports allocation, waiting reason and exhaustion' for shared resource allocation, so the word will exist twice in the system with two meanings: waiting for a Provider and waiting for a slot in the shared allocation. Two enums with overlapping members is how an owner comes to read one as the other, and a single merged enum would have to answer questions from both domains and would eventually gain a member neither owns. Deriving the members from the table cells rather than writing a plausible list is what makes totality checkable: a cell with no reason and a reason with no cell are both test failures, which is the same discipline V2-067's TestProviderRegistryFailureClassMapIsTotal already applies to the health mapping.

decisions.decision: What a fixture can show and what only V2-028 can show is split explicitly, and the split is written into the evidence before any code. Fixtures and unit tests here establish: the compatibility decision total over its inputs with an explicit unknown; the three cli-version-incompatible fixtures producing contract-incompatible for all three adapters and the resulting open being immediate, probe-ineligible and closable only by an observed version change; the disposition table total and deterministic; the target filters enforcing authorization, compatibility and the attempt history; and that a chosen disposition preserves the handoff content digest across all six ordered Provider pairs with a refusal on any loss. V2-028 alone establishes: that a declared interval is TRUE of a real CLI; that a real exhaustion or a real contract break produces the class the table assumes; that a real handoff preserves the Increment, Artifact and Evidence through a real journal, lease and Evidence record; and that the waiting reason an owner sees in Preview is the one the capability's journey requires.
decisions.rationale: V2-027 already drew this exact line for M6's condition 3 and its evidence states the halves: it proved 'fixture-level preservation and a fail-closed refusal on loss -- a content digest over IncrementID, Constraints, Decisions, Artifacts, Verification and Unresolved, asserted for all six ordered pairs of the three Provider names, with twelve distinct mutations each producing a refusal' and attributed 'preservation through a real switch with a real journal, lease, Increment and Evidence record' to V2-028. This task adds the decision in front of that machinery, so its fixture half is 'the decision does not lose anything the conversion already preserves' and its live half is unchanged and still V2-028's. Stating it before writing code is what stops the evidence from drifting into claiming the live half, which G3.3 forbids at any grade. There is also a hard practical bound to record: two of the three CLIs have no authenticated session on this machine, so no real handoff between two real Providers is performable by any agent -- authenticating a CLI uses the owner's own identity -- which makes the live half owner-blocked and not merely deferred.

decisions.decision: V2-074 is IN the surface-widening serialization chain and should be inserted immediately after V2-068, giving V2-073 (running) to V2-068 to V2-074 to V2-065 to V2-072. Issuing the id and confirming the position is the coordinator's.
decisions.rationale: It touches four of the six chain file groups -- internal/application's read models and service, contracts/openapi/openapi-v1.yaml, internal/web/owner.{html,js} and internal/api's response assertions -- so it cannot avoid the chain; d11 keeps both store adapters out, which is why it is four and not six. The position is determined by two dependencies on V2-068, both measured. First, V2-068 replaces the reported concurrency ceiling: ProviderCeilingSource has exactly one member today because exactly one source exists (internal/application/provider_registry.go:331-337) and dp-v2-067 d11 assigns the installation-settable limit and its own member to V2-068. concurrency.exhausted is one of this task's Sendable inputs, so landing first would pin the disposition table against a design ceiling that V2-068 then replaces, forcing the table to be re-verified. Second, V2-068 introduces the queue waiting reason that d12 must be asserted disjoint from; that assertion cannot be written before the other vocabulary exists. Landing after V2-068 makes both inputs final.

risks: The decision table exists twice, in internal/provider and in internal/application, because application may not import provider. The by-value pinning test is the only thing that will catch drift, and it can only compare the shared normalised tuple, not the two mappings onto it. If one side's mapping is later widened without the other's, the pinning test still passes while the two disagree. The mitigation is that each mapping must be asserted total over its own closed enums, so a new enum member fails a test on the side that gained it.

The pre-invocation compatibility refusal is armed only when a caller supplies Request.CLIVersionDeclared, and no production caller supplies it, because internal/runner is deliberately untouched. The refusal is therefore exercised by tests and not by production, and the evidence must say so in those words. A reader who takes the surface as proof that an incompatible CLI cannot be invoked would be wrong, and naming the owner of arming it is the only honest mitigation.

The residual from d7 stands: RequestFromHandoff keeps its signature, so a caller who hand-picks a target and calls it directly can still reach a Provider whose slot is unauthenticated. The AST single-caller guard is what makes that unreachable in this tree, and a guard is weaker than a signature. It was chosen only because widening the signature would stop existing tests compiling under their own names.

The observed-CLI side of the verdict is permanently unknown until a Runner client exists, because no observed version reaches the control plane and widening the observation DTO would turn an existing test red. The surface therefore reports the declared intervals plus an unknown, and a reader may take unknown as compatible. The mitigation is V2-069's rule applied literally: unknown is a sibling value of compatible in the same closed enum, rendered with its reason, and never a default.

Two of the three Provider CLIs have no authenticated session on this machine and no agent can create one, so a real handoff between two real Providers cannot be exercised at all in this task or in any task before the owner authenticates a second CLI. The live half of the capability is owner-blocked rather than merely deferred, and the evidence must record it as an escalation with the owner named.

Editing contracts/openapi/openapi-v1.yaml moves the contracts component key, which is a declared contract dependency of the api and control-plane components, and the new blocks land inside schemas that set additionalProperties:false, so every added field is forced to be declared. Only the provider, application and api evidence records are issued here; the remaining key movement is a note for V2-045 under gate rule G6.

The new blocks must pass two independent existing vocabulary scans -- V2-067's ban on budget, quota, billing, spend, cost and credit over the emitted read-model JSON keys, and internal/provider's ban on usd, cost, price, billing, spend, budget and credit over declared identifiers. A field named for a usage ceiling is the obvious way to trip both, and the design's answer is that no ceiling value and no threshold number appears in the block at all: only which side of the line the window is on.
